items.title: Registered slash commands can silently have no CLI dispatch branch (/whoami, /indicator)

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary

`COMMAND_REGISTRY` in `hermes_cli/commands.py` is the single source of truth for `/help`,
tab completion, and the Telegram/Discord command menus. The classic CLI, however, dispatches
slash commands from a hand-written if/elif chain inside `HermesCLI.process_command`
(`cli.py`, ~691 lines as of 8eb06e75b9).

Nothing keeps the two in sync. A command can be registered — and therefore advertised in
`/help` and offered by autocomplete — while `process_command` has no branch for it. The user
types it, and nothing happens. No error, no "unknown command": it falls through to the
quick-command/skill fallback and is silently swallowed.

This is not hypothetical. Two commands are in that state on `main` right now, and each already
has a separate PR fixing it individually:

| Command | Registry flags | State |
|---|---|---|
| `whoami` | none — CLI **and** gateway | no CLI dispatch branch → #26047 |
| `indicator` | `cli_only=True` — CLI **only** | no CLI dispatch branch at all → #41869 |

`indicator` is the clearer illustration: it is marked `cli_only`, so the CLI is the only place
it can possibly run, and the CLI does not handle it.

## Reproduce

From a repo checkout at `main`:

```bash
python3 -c '
import re
src = open("hermes_cli/commands.py").read()
names = re.findall(r"CommandDef\(\s*\"([^\"]+)\"", src)
cli = open("cli.py").read()
body = cli[cli.index("def process_command("):][:40000]
print([n for n in names if f"\"{n}\"" not in body and f"/{n}" not in body])'
```

```
['start', 'topic', 'approve', 'deny', 'whoami', 'sethome', 'indicator', 'restart', 'platform']
```

Seven of those nine are `gateway_only=True` and correctly absent from the CLI dispatcher.
The two that are not — `whoami` and `indicator` — are the bugs above.

Interactively: launch the classic CLI, type `/ind<TAB>`. Completion offers `/indicator`
(it comes from the registry). Run it: nothing happens.

## Why this keeps happening

The two open PRs are treating the symptom one command at a time. The root cause is structural:
adding a command means editing two unrelated places, and only one of them is enforced. There is
no test asserting that a registered, CLI-reachable command is actually reachable. `process_command`
being a ~691-line if/elif chain makes the omission easy to make and hard to see in review.

## Proposal

Add a parity test as a guardrail first — independent of, and non-conflicting with, #26047 and
#41869:

- Walk `COMMAND_REGISTRY`, skip `gateway_only=True`, and assert each remaining command (or one of
  its aliases) is referenced inside `process_command`.
- Ship it with a small allowlist holding exactly `whoami` and `indicator`, each annotated with its
  PR link, so the test is **green on current `main`** and does not touch either in-flight fix. When
  those PRs merge, deleting the allowlist entries makes the check total.
- Include a companion assertion that fails if an allowlisted command *does* gain a dispatch branch,
  so the allowlist cannot quietly outlive its entries.

Deliberately permissive: it looks for the command name anywhere in the function body rather than
trying to recognise branch shapes, so it has no false positives while still catching the actual
failure mode (a command being entirely absent).

Happy to open that PR. Longer term, the dispatch could hang off `CommandDef` itself — a `handler`
field on the existing registry, so registration and dispatch are one edit instead of two — but
that is a separate, incremental discussion and not needed to close this.

items.title: Nix build: hermes_state_* modules missing from pyproject py-modules — TUI errors and gateway crash-loops

labels.name: area/nix
labels.description: Nix flake, NixOS module, container packaging

items.body:
Same bug class as #5502: root-level Python modules not declared in `[tool.setuptools] py-modules`, so the uv2nix wheel build silently excludes them. The pip/curl install path is unaffected (runs from the repo tree), which is why this only surfaces on Nix.

**Environment:** NixOS, `nix profile add github:NousResearch/hermes-agent` @ main (2026-07-29), Hermes Agent v0.19.0.

**Symptoms:**
- `hermes --tui` → `error: agent init failed: No module named 'hermes_state_common'` (plain `hermes` CLI works)
- `hermes gateway run` (systemd unit from `hermes gateway install`) crash-loops:
  ```
  [gateway] Warning: SQLite session store unavailable, falling back to JSONL: No module named 'hermes_state_portability'
  systemd[..]: hermes-gateway.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
  ```

**Undeclared root modules** (checked `*.py` at repo root vs the py-modules list):
`hermes_state_common`, `hermes_state_portability`, `hermes_state_schema`, `hermes_state_search` (and `mini_swe_runner`, if it's meant to ship).

**Fix (verified locally — TUI and gateway both work after rebuilding from a patched clone):**
```diff
-py-modules = [... "hermes_state", "hermes_time", ...]
+py-modules = [... "hermes_state", "hermes_state_common", "hermes_state_portability", "hermes_state_schema", "hermes_state_search", "hermes_time", ...]
```

Suggestion: a CI check that compares root `*.py` files against `py-modules` would prevent this class of regression (this is its second occurrence after #5502).

items.body:
> **Disclosure**: This issue was drafted by an AI assistant (Kimi, by Moonshot AI) acting on behalf of the affected user, with the user's review and explicit permission at every step of the process. The user operates the GitHub account submitting this issue and takes responsibility for it. All technical content below was verified against the user's local installation logs and the repository's git history.

## Bug 1: `pyproject.toml` py-modules omits modules introduced by 21c7ae856

Commit `21c7ae856` ("refactor: split SessionDB into Search/Schema/Portability mixins") added four new top-level modules, and `mini_swe_runner.py` also exists at repo root, but none of them are registered in `[tool.setuptools] py-modules`:

- `hermes_state_common.py`
- `hermes_state_portability.py`
- `hermes_state_schema.py`
- `hermes_state_search.py`
- `mini_swe_runner.py`

Current line 349 of `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
py-modules = ["run_agent", "model_tools", "toolsets", "batch_runner", "trajectory_compressor", "toolset_distributions", "cli", "hermes_bootstrap", "hermes_constants", "hermes_state", "hermes_time", "hermes_logging", "utils", "mcp_serve"]
```

### Impact

Any fresh `uv pip install -e .` / venv rebuild produces an environment where `import hermes_state` hard-fails:

```
File ".../hermes_state.py", line 45, in <module>
    from hermes_state_common import (  # noqa: F401  (re-exported for back-compat)
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'hermes_state_common'
```

After adding `hermes_state_common`, the next missing one surfaces (`hermes_state_portability`), etc. The gateway cannot start from such an environment; `hermes_cli.managed_uv` smoke checks report `candidate venv smoke failed: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'hermes_state_common'`.

### Suggested fix

```toml
py-modules = ["run_agent", "model_tools", "toolsets", "batch_runner", "trajectory_compressor", "toolset_distributions", "cli", "hermes_bootstrap", "hermes_constants", "hermes_state", "hermes_state_common", "hermes_state_portability", "hermes_state_schema", "hermes_state_search", "mini_swe_runner", "hermes_time", "hermes_logging", "utils", "mcp_serve"]
```

Verified locally: after adding these five names and reinstalling editable, `import hermes_state, hermes_cli, run_agent, gateway` all succeed and the gateway boots cleanly.

## Bug 2: bootstrap updater recreates venv while its own gateway processes still hold file locks

Observed on Windows 11, hermes-agent v0.19.0 (upstream `98e43be8e`), managed install via `hermes-setup.exe`.

### What happened

During a routine update at 2026-07-30 13:41-13:43 local time, the bootstrap installer:

1. fast-forwarded the repo (`ba7d214b6..98e43be8e`) successfully,
2. entered the `venv` stage ("Virtual environment already exists, recreating..."),
3. failed to delete a locked file because the still-running hermes gateway (spawned earlier by the same installation) held it open:

```
bootstrap FAILED stage=Some("venv") error=Access to the path '...hermes-agent\venv\Lib\site-packages\cryptography\hazmat\bindings\_rust.pyd' is denied.
```

### Impact

The venv was left half-deleted:

- `site-packages/hermes_agent/` was removed (uninstalled) while `hermes_agent-0.19.0.dist-info` remained,
- entry-point executables were renamed to stale backups (`hermes.exe.old.1785390099976`, `hermes-agent.exe.old.*`, `hermes-acp.exe.old.*`),
- `.update-incomplete` marker left behind,
- `hermes.exe` / gateway effectively dead until manual repair (kill leftover `gateway run` processes, `uv venv --clear`, editable reinstall).

### Suggestion

Before recreating the venv, the bootstrap/update flow should stop (or refuse to run alongside) any running `hermes_cli.main gateway run` / agent processes that have files open inside the install tree — or stage the new venv beside the old one and swap atomically, so a failed stage never leaves the install without working entry points.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- hermes-agent: v0.19.0 (2026.7.20), upstream commit `98e43be8e`
- Install method: git (managed via hermes-setup.exe bootstrap)
- Python: 3.11.15 (uv-managed)

items.title: [Bug]: OpenViking: after the first in-place compression, a session can never be committed again — post-compression turns are never extracted

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

The OpenViking memory provider tracks committed session ids in an in-memory set (`_committed_session_ids`): once a session id has been committed, every later commit attempt for that same id is silently rejected — the guard explicitly wins over the turn counter, so newly arrived turns do not re-arm it.

Context compression (auto or manual `/compress` — both share the single `compress_context()` entry) always calls `commit_memory_session()` before rewriting the transcript. What happens next depends entirely on the compression mode:

- **Rotation mode (`compression.in_place: false`) — works correctly.** The commit fires for the *old* session id, then compression mints a *new* session id and the provider rotates to it. The new id starts clean (not in the committed set), so the next compression or session end commits normally. The chain stays healthy across any number of compressions. The only side effect: each compression adds a `name #N` continuation row to the `/resume` session list.
- **In-place mode (`compression.in_place: true` — the DEFAULT) — broken.** The session id does **not** change. The first compression commits it successfully and lands the id in the committed set; from that point on, every commit attempt for this still-live session — subsequent compressions, `/new`, normal session end, startup recovery — is rejected by the guard. All turns produced **after** the first compression keep syncing to OpenViking as pending tokens but are **never extracted into memories**.

Net effect with default config: any session that compresses once is extracted **at most once** in its lifetime. This affects all frontends (CLI, TUI, desktop, messaging gateway) because the logic lives in the agent core and the provider, not in any frontend.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Use any frontend (CLI/TUI/desktop) with OpenViking as the memory provider, default config (`compression.in_place: true`).
2. Chat until context compression fires (auto or manual `/compress`). → First commit succeeds: `OpenViking session <sid> committed on session end (N turns)`.
3. Continue chatting more turns in the same session.
4. Trigger a second compression, then end the session properly (`/new` in CLI, or close in TUI).

### Expected Behavior

Turns produced after the first compression are extracted too — either by the second compression, or at the latest when the session ends properly. Every turn's content eventually lands in the OpenViking knowledge base.

### Actual Behavior

The second compression and the session end produce **no** commit. The session is extracted exactly once (at first compression); everything after that is permanently lost to memory. Observed in `agent.log`: one `committed on session end` line for the sid at the first compression, then multiple later `in_place_committed` compression telemetry events with no further OpenViking commit lines.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Debug report uploaded:
  Report       https://paste.rs/2HE9w
  agent.log    https://dpaste.com/8ZHDFH73G
  gateway.log  https://paste.rs/baWqP
  gui.log      https://paste.rs/ooCOm
  desktop.log  https://paste.rs/qZ3Ah
```

### Operating System

windows 11

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.19.0 (2026.7.20) · upstream 866c9ad

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

**1. Compression always attempts a commit — in both modes.** `agent/conversation_compression.py:2059-2063` (single chokepoint `compress_context()`, reached by auto compression from `conversation_loop.py:1888/4225` and by manual `/compress` alike):

```python
# Trigger memory extraction on the current session before the
# transcript is rewritten (runs in BOTH modes — the logical
# conversation's pre-compaction turns are about to be summarized
# away regardless of whether the id rotates).
agent.commit_memory_session(messages)
```

**2. The committed-guard is a boolean per sid, in provider memory, and explicitly wins over new turns.** `plugins/memory/openviking/__init__.py:2993`:

```python
def _session_needs_commit(self, sid: str, turn_count: int) -> bool:
    # Already-committed sessions never need a second commit, regardless of
    # the turn counter — a racing sync_turn can re-increment _turn_count
    # after a commit+reset, so the committed-guard must win over turn_count.
    if self._has_committed_session(sid):
        return False
    if turn_count > 0:
        return True
    return self._session_has_pending_tokens(sid)
```

`_committed_session_ids` is a plain in-memory set (`__init__.py:2711-2717`); a successful commit adds the sid and resets `_turn_count` to 0 (`__init__.py:4127-4131`).

**3. In-place mode keeps the same sid, so the guard applies to the live session.** With `compression.in_place: true` (the default, `agent/agent_init.py:1963`), `on_session_switch` is called with the **same** sid and does not rotate:

```python
# plugins/memory/openviking/__init__.py:4172
rotate = not (rewound or new_id == old_session_id)   # same sid → no rotation
```

From then on the sid is in `_committed_session_ids`, so `_session_needs_commit` returns False for every later attempt — including the real session end. Post-compression turns re-increment `_turn_count` via `sync_turn`, but the guard "must win over turn_count" by design.

**4. Rotation mode (`in_place: false`) does NOT have this problem** — which confirms the guard's intent was only to prevent a racing double-commit of the *same* old sid. In rotation mode a fresh child sid is minted (`conversation_compression.py:2143`), the provider rotates to it (`on_session_switch` → `rotate=True`), and the new sid starts clean: it commits normally at the next boundary. The guard then correctly dedupes the old sid's second finalize (`_finalize_session_async` at `__init__.py:4196`) against the compression commit.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

_No response_

items.title: Desktop: checkpoint restore fails with 'target user message is no longer in session history'

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Context

When restoring to a checkpoint in the Hermes desktop app, the user gets the error "target user message is no longer in session history" even though the target message is visible in the session transcript. The issue is a counting mismatch: the desktop client computes `truncate_before_user_ordinal` by filtering on `!hidden`, but the server filters on `!display_kind`. These produce different counts when user messages carry `display_kind` markers (skill_invocation, auto_continue, model_switch, etc.), causing the client ordinal to exceed the server-valid range.

The server check (`tui_gateway/methods_prompt.py` line 166-176):
```python
user_indices = [
    i for i, m in enumerate(history)
    if m.get("role") == "user" and not m.get("display_kind")
]
if ordinal < 0 or ordinal >= len(user_indices):
    return _err(rid, 4018, "target user message is no longer in session history")
```

The client computation (`apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/utils.ts` line 363-365):
```ts
export function visibleUserOrdinal(messages: readonly ChatMessage[], end: number): number {
  return messages.slice(0, end).filter(m => m.role === "user" && !m.hidden).length
}
```

`hidden` is set on assistant branch messages; `display_kind` is set on special user turns (skill invocations, auto-continuations, etc.). The client has no way to know about `display_kind` since it is stripped from the `ChatMessage[]` type.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] **A1: Checkpoint restore succeeds for sessions containing skill-invoked user turns** — Given a session where user messages have `display_kind` markers, When the user restores to any visible user message checkpoint, Then the restore succeeds without error.

- [ ] **A2: Checkpoint restore succeeds for sessions with auto-continue messages** — Given a session with `display_kind: "auto_continue"` user turns, When the user restores to any checkpoint, Then the `truncate_before_user_ordinal` value is within the server-valid range.

- [ ] **A3: Ordinal computation uses the same filter as the server** — The client-side ordinal for a given message matches the server-side count of real user turns (excluding `display_kind` messages).

- [ ] **A4: Restoring to the first user turn works in all session shapes** — Given any session shape, When the user restores to the first user message, Then the server accepts the ordinal 0 (with `confirm_empty_truncate: true`).

- [ ] **A5: Restoring to the last user turn works in all session shapes** — Given any session shape, When the user restores to the last user message, Then the server accepts the computed ordinal.

## Scope

- Fix the client-side ordinal computation to match the server-side counting logic.

## Out of scope

- Adding new API parameters (e.g. message-id-based truncation).
- Changes to the server-side counting logic.
- Changes to the TUI restore path.

## Dependencies

None.

## File plan

* **MODIFY:** `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/utils.ts` — Update `visibleUserOrdinal` or add a new function that computes ordinal using `display_kind` instead of `hidden`.
* **MODIFY:** `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/rewind.ts` — Update `planRestore` to use the corrected ordinal computation.
* **MODIFY:** `apps/desktop/src/lib/chat-messages.ts` — Add `displayKind` field to `ChatMessage` type if not already present, so the ordinal computation has access to this data.
* **MODIFY:** `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/rewind.test.ts` — Add tests for sessions with `display_kind` markers on user messages.
* **MODIFY:** `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-prompt-actions/index.test.tsx` — Add regression tests for checkpoint restore with skill turns.

## Contract

The `ChatMessage` type needs to carry `displayKind: SessionMessage['display_kind'] | null`. This is populated during session resume from the gateway response. The `visibleUserOrdinal` function (or a replacement) must filter on `!display_kind` instead of `!hidden`.

## Locked decisions

- Fix is in the client ordinal computation, not the server.
- No new API parameter — keep using `truncate_before_user_ordinal`.
- The `ChatMessage` type must carry `displayKind` from the server response.

## Self-validation procedure

1. Read the issue end-to-end. Confirm the File plan matches the codebase.
2. Add `displayKind` to `ChatMessage` type and ensure it is populated during session resume.
3. Update `visibleUserOrdinal` to filter on `!displayKind` instead of `!hidden`.
4. Run existing tests — all must pass.
5. Add tests for the regression case (session with `display_kind` user turns).
6. Re-run A1 through A5 by testing the desktop restore flow in sessions with skill turns.
7. Run `make check` (or the project validation command) and confirm all checks pass.
8. Report back with the assertion table and commit SHAs.

## Execution notes

- Stop and report if any A## is unsatisfiable — do not weaken an assertion to make a failing test pass.

items.title: Desktop: no unpin affordance for pinned sessions + silent pin-capacity limit

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Bug Summary

Two related issues with session pinning in the Desktop sidebar:

### 1. No unpin affordance

Once a session is pinned in the sidebar, there is no obvious or working way to unpin it. The following actions were tried and none produced an unpin:
- Right-click context menu on a pinned session — no unpin option present
- Shift+Click on an already-pinned session — no effect
- Cmd+K / Command Palette — no unpin command found
- Looking for dedicated UI (pin icon toggle, close button, etc.) — none visible

### 2. Silent pin-capacity limit

There appears to be an undocumented, unseen limit on how many sessions can be pinned at once. After pinning approximately N sessions (observed in the low dozens), additional pin attempts silently fail — the session appears to pin momentarily but reverts, or simply does not stick. There is no UI indicator (toast, counter, hover text) anywhere in the sidebar or session panel that communicates:
- How many sessions are currently pinned
- Whether a limit exists
- What the limit is
- Whether the user is approaching or has hit it

This makes the feature effectively unusable for anyone who wants to maintain a curated workspace of active sessions.

## Expected Behavior

1. **Unpin affordance:** Pinned sessions should have a clear, discoverable way to unpin — whether via:
   - A right-click context menu "Unpin" entry
   - A toggle/pin icon in the session row that switches between pin/unpin
   - A Cmd+K command like "Unpin current session" or "Unpin session..."
2. **Pin limit transparency:**
   - If a limit exists, it should be documented in the UI (e.g., a small badge or tooltip showing "12 / 25 pinned")
   - When the limit is reached, attempting to pin more should show a clear message (e.g., "Maximum of 25 pinned sessions reached. Unpin others first.")
   - Better yet, either remove the cap or raise it to a generous default

## Actual Behavior

Pinning feels like a one-way door — sessions go in but can't come out of the pinned state, and the side effect of hitting an invisible ceiling means users unknowingly lose the ability to pin new sessions, with no error or feedback.

## Environment

- Hermes Desktop (latest)
- macOS 26.5.2 (Sequoia)
- Session sidebar

## Related

- #74570 — pin/unpin silently reverted by pullRemotePins race (separate issue; this one is about missing UX affordance and invisible capacity limits)

items.title: Desktop update loops forever: updater refuses the marker the desktop pre-wrote with the updater's own PID

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

On macOS, the Desktop in-app update can never complete: the updater refuses to run because it sees an update-in-progress marker whose PID is **its own**. The desktop then relaunches, re-triggers the update, and the cycle repeats indefinitely.

`live_marker_owner()` has no self-PID exclusion, but since #50238 the desktop writes the marker *on the updater's behalf, using the updater's PID*, before the updater reaches `run_update`. So `UpdateMarkerGuard::acquire()` reads a marker owned by a live PID — itself — and bails out.

## Environment

- macOS 15 (Darwin 25.1.0), Apple Silicon
- Install method: `git` (`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`), tracking `NousResearch/hermes-agent`
- Observed on checkouts around `9accf79d8` … `19556db61` (0.19.0 mid-cycle, 2026-07-30)
- Backend: remote gateway (desktop connects to a self-hosted backend, not a local one)

## Symptom

`~/.hermes/logs/bootstrap-installer.log`, one full iteration:

```
09:56:26.199606Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib: Hermes installer starting mode=Update force_setup=false
09:56:26.671851Z  INFO bootstrap.log: [update] waiting for Hermes to exit… stage=update
09:56:26.679758Z  INFO bootstrap.log: [update] updating against branch main stage=update
09:56:28.003626Z  INFO bootstrap.log: ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 10198, started 2s ago). stage=update
09:56:28.032112Z  INFO ...update: update stage stage=update state=Failed duration_ms=Some(1352)
                  error=Some("Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again.")
```

`~/.hermes/logs/desktop.log` shows the other half of the loop — each iteration takes a fresh emergency `state.db` backup, so the retries are easy to count:

```
[updates] restart: Updating Hermes — this window will close and the updater will open.
[updates] state.db pre-flight: size=151552, headerOk=true
[updates] emergency state.db backup: ~/.hermes/state.db.pre-update-emergency-2026-07-30T09-40-51-194Z.bak
[updates] launched updater: ~/.hermes/hermes-setup --update --branch main --target-app …/Hermes.app; exiting desktop to release venv shim
[boot] Resolving Hermes backend
[boot] Connecting to remote Hermes backend at https://…
[boot] Remote Hermes backend is ready
[updates] restart: Updating Hermes — this window will close and the updater will open.   <-- loops
```

Key detail: **only one `Hermes installer starting` line appears per iteration**, and the PID named in the collision message matches the PID in `~/.hermes/.hermes-update-in-progress`. There is no second updater process — the reported "other" updater is the reporting process itself. The 1–2s age matches the gap between the desktop's `spawn()` and the updater reaching `run_update`.

## Root cause

1. `apps/desktop/electron/update-marker.ts` → `writeUpdateMarker(hermesHome, pid)` is called by the desktop immediately after `spawn()` of `hermes-setup --update`, with **the spawned updater's PID**. Its own doc comment anticipates the overwrite:

   > The updater's `UpdateMarkerGuard` will later overwrite it with its own PID — that's fine, the marker body is the same format and `readLiveUpdateMarker` only cares that *some* live pid owns it.

   That holds for the Electron-side reader, but not for the Rust-side *writer*, which must first acquire.

2. `apps/bootstrap-installer/src-tauri/src/update.rs`:

```rust
fn acquire(path: PathBuf) -> Result<Self, MarkerOwner> {
    if let Some(owner) = live_marker_owner(&path) {
        return Err(owner);          // <-- owner.pid == std::process::id()
    }
    let pid = std::process::id();
    ...
}

fn live_marker_owner(path: &Path) -> Option<MarkerOwner> {
    ...
    if age_secs > UPDATE_MARKER_MAX_AGE_SECS || !pid_is_alive(pid) {
        return None;
    }
    Some(MarkerOwner { pid, age_secs })   // no `pid == std::process::id()` check
}
```

The marker is fresh (2s, under the ceiling) and the PID is alive (it is the caller), so `acquire()` returns `Err` and `run_update` aborts before ever overwriting the marker.

The age ceiling (`UPDATE_MARKER_MAX_AGE_SECS`) does eventually self-heal this, but only after 20 minutes, during which every attempt fails the same way.

## Suggested fix

Treat the current process as a non-owner — one line in `live_marker_owner` (or in `acquire` before the `Err` return):

```rust
if pid == std::process::id() {
    return None;   // our own marker, pre-written by the desktop at spawn (#50238)
}
```

This preserves the mutual-exclusion intent (a *foreign* live updater, e.g. a dashboard-spawned `hermes update`, still blocks) while letting the updater adopt the marker the desktop wrote for it. A regression test alongside `acquire_refuses_while_a_live_updater_owns_the_marker()` — "acquire adopts a marker containing our own pid" — would pin it.

## Workaround

Close all Hermes windows, delete the marker, and run the updater from a terminal:

```bash
rm -f ~/.hermes/.hermes-update-in-progress
~/.hermes/hermes-setup --update --branch main
```

With no desktop instance to pre-write the marker, `acquire()` succeeds and the update completes normally (verified twice today, both stages `Succeeded`).

## Secondary observation

Across two successful updates pulling 31 commits total, the rebuild stage exited in ~1.2s both times with `✓ Desktop packaged app is up to date (content stamp matches)`, while `desktop-build-stamp.json` did get a new `contentHash` and `builtAt`. If the stamp is recomputed from the *source* rather than compared against what the packaged app was built from, the bundle could silently go stale. Not investigated further — flagging in case it is related.

items.title: Recover Gemini's textual tool-call leak (declaration:default_api…) instead of streaming it as assistant content

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
## Problem

When a run targets a Gemini model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway (LiteLLM in our case),
Gemini intermittently emits its function call as **plain text content** instead of a native
`tool_calls` entry, in its internal DSL:

```
declaration:default_api:cet outil{demandes:[{assistant:…,demande:…}]}
```

hermes-agent (0.19.0) has no recognition of this signature (neither `declaration:default_api`
nor the older `tool_code` marker appear anywhere in the agent code). The leak is streamed
verbatim to the end user as the assistant's answer — pseudo-code instead of a response — and the
tool is never executed.

Two facts that took us a while to establish, offered here to save you the time:

- **It is non-deterministic on an identical setup.** Same container boot, same profile, same
  tool list: native tool call at 07:39, textual leak at 08:12. Frequency seems to grow with the
  size of the tool list (~47 tools) and of the system prompt.
- **It is not the gateway.** The same model alias called directly through LiteLLM with the same
  tool schema produced native `tool_calls` 3/3, including with reasoning enabled. The difference
  is the request shape built by the agent loop (many tools + long system + streaming).

Also for the record: the periodic `Failed to fetch model metadata from OpenRouter` warning in
air-gapped deployments is unrelated — `model_metadata.py` only drives context length and vision,
not tool support. We chased that first; dead end.

## Proposal

In the response-handling path (where `_sanitize_tool_call_arguments` and the message-sequence
repairs already live), when an assistant message has **no `tool_calls`** and its content, after
leading whitespace, starts with `declaration:default_api`:

1. parse the tool name and arguments from the DSL (it is close to JSON5 — unquoted keys);
2. convert the message into a proper assistant `tool_calls` entry and execute as usual;
3. on unparseable payloads, fall back to a retry of the completion (the non-determinism makes a
   single retry very likely to succeed) rather than surfacing the DSL to the user.

A config flag to disable the recovery keeps the current behavior available.

## Notes

- Happy to contribute the repro: an OpenAI-compatible profile with ~45 tool definitions against
  `google/gemini-*` via LiteLLM reproduces the leak within a few dozen turns.
- Related well-known Gemini behavior: the `tool_code`/`default_api` leak family reported across
  ecosystems; hermes is simply missing a recovery for it, its other repair machinery is exactly
  where this belongs.

items.title: Desktop SSH profiles cannot target a differently named remote profile

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Problem

Hermes Desktop uses the selected Desktop profile name as the remote Hermes profile when a profile-scoped SSH connection starts a managed backend.

That assumption breaks a valid multi-machine layout where the Desktop profile is a local routing label and the target installation uses a different profile name.

For example:

```text
Desktop profile: workstation-agent
SSH host: remote-box
Remote Hermes profile: default
```

Desktop currently launches the remote backend with `--profile workstation-agent`. If the remote installation only has `default`, the backend exits with `Profile 'workstation-agent' does not exist`. Desktop then commonly reports the secondary and misleading ownership error instead of the actual profile mismatch.

The workaround is to create a duplicate remote profile purely to match the local label, or make SSH global. The first duplicates profile state; the second replaces the local profile inventory and defeats local/remote coexistence.

## Reproduction

1. Keep Hermes Desktop's global connection in Local mode.
2. Create a named Desktop profile such as `workstation-agent`.
3. Configure a profile-scoped SSH connection for it.
4. On the remote host, keep only the `default` Hermes profile.
5. Connect from the Desktop profile.

Desktop forwards `workstation-agent` to the remote `hermes --profile` argument, and the managed backend exits because that remote profile does not exist.

## Expected behavior

A named Desktop SSH override should optionally map its local scope to an explicit remote Hermes profile:

```text
workstation-agent -> SSH remote-box -> default
```

If the mapping is blank or absent, Desktop should preserve the existing same-name behavior for backward compatibility.

The mapping must also participate in SSH bootstrap identity and backend reuse. Changing the remote profile must not reuse a managed backend created for a different profile.

## Proposed UI and configuration

For named SSH scopes, add **Remote profile (optional)** under Settings -> Gateway.

```json
{
  "profiles": {
    "workstation-agent": {
      "mode": "ssh",
      "host": "remote-box",
      "remoteProfile": "default"
    }
  }
}
```

Blank means "use the Desktop profile name." An explicit blank must also clear a previously saved mapping.

## Related issues

- #37876 tracks the broader local/remote coexistence design. Per-profile overrides now cover most of it, but they still assume matching profile names for SSH.
- #69551 and duplicate #74090 cover a different named-profile failure: profile-scoped token-path validation. Fixing that allows named remote profiles to start, but does not let a local routing label target a differently named remote profile.

I have a tested implementation ready and will link the PR.

items.body:
## Summary

`_adapter_for_source` is used for two purposes with **opposite** failure requirements:

- **authorization / intake** — must fail closed, so an intake decision never leaks across profiles
- **outbound delivery** — must fall back, or the user never receives the message

In a `multiplex_profiles` deployment that serves a profile owning no adapter for the platform a turn arrived on, the resolver returns `None` (correct for authorization), and the approval/status delivery path then dereferences it.

## Observed (0.18.2)

```
tools.approval: Gateway approval notify failed:
  'NoneType' object has no attribute 'pause_typing_for_chat'
```

Effect: the interactive approval prompt is never delivered, so `approval.py` returns `BLOCKED: Failed to send approval request to user`. The practical consequence is worse than one lost message — the agent can still run command patterns approved earlier in the session, but **any new pattern becomes unapprovable**, with no path for the user to grant it. It looks like a policy gate and is actually a delivery failure.

## Still present on `main` (0.19.0)

`gateway/run.py:4663` and `gateway/run.py:4814`:

```python
ctx._status_adapter.pause_typing_for_chat(ctx._status_chat_id)
```

Neither is guarded against `_status_adapter` being `None`.

## How we reached it

To be upfront: downstream we run a keyword router that stamps `source.profile` on a turn which arrived on the **default** profile's channel, so config/memory/tools/cwd follow a per-user pointer — and the routed profile deliberately has no adapter of its own. That router is not upstream.

The resolver conflation and the unguarded dereference are upstream, though, and any deployment where a served profile lacks an adapter for the receiving platform can reach the same state. The `None` return is intentional and correct; the delivery path's assumption that it can't happen is the bug.

## Suggested direction

Split the two concerns rather than changing the existing resolver's bias:

1. Keep `_adapter_for_source` exactly as-is — fail-closed — for intake, authorization and queue management.
2. Add a delivery-only resolver: try the profile-scoped adapter first (so a profile that *does* own its door keeps using it), else fall back to the default/active profile's same-platform adapter, else `None`.
3. Use the delivery resolver **only** at genuinely outbound sites — status, typing, clarify, approval, reply sends — and leave intake / authz / queue / interrupt / restore / platform-control sites on the fail-closed one.
4. Guard the dereference regardless, so a fully unresolvable adapter degrades to a clean logged failure naming profile and platform, instead of an `AttributeError`.

Point 3 is the fiddly part: the two categories are easy to mix up, and switching an authorization site would silently weaken it.

## What we did

Implemented the above on 0.18.2: a `_delivery_adapter_for_source` helper in `gateway/authz_mixin.py`, ~34 outbound sites switched, 24 left fail-closed, the dereference guarded, plus a regression test covering: doorless profile delivers via the receiving adapter while authorization still returns `None`; a profile owning its adapter keeps using it; default-profile behaviour unchanged; `None` source, missing platform and unmapped platform all degrade to `None` without raising.

Happy to open a PR if the direction is welcome — with the caveat that the call-site set changed noticeably between 0.18.2 and 0.19.0 (the status/approval path moved onto a context object), so it would need porting rather than cherry-picking.

items.body:
**Describe the bug**

`/model` (picking/switching a model) freezes for 13–15 seconds before showing the provider/model list when `models.dev` is unreachable from the user’s network.

This affects users behind the Great Firewall of China, corporate firewalls, air-gapped environments, or any network where `models.dev` is blocked.

**To Reproduce**

1. Be on a network where `https://models.dev/api.json` is unreachable (e.g. mainland China, corporate VPN, no outbound internet)
2. Run `hermes` and type `/model`
3. Wait 13–15 seconds with a frozen terminal before the picker appears

**Expected behavior**

The model picker should appear in <2 seconds, falling back to the local disk cache immediately instead of waiting for a network timeout.

**Root cause**

`agent/models_dev.py:293`:
```python
response = requests.get(MODELS_DEV_URL, timeout=15)
```

`fetch_models_dev()` does a synchronous 15-second HTTP GET to `https://models.dev/api.json`. When this host is unreachable, the function blocks for the full timeout before falling back to disk cache.

**Impact**

- Users behind restricted networks get a 13–15s freeze on every `/model` invocation
- `model_catalog.enabled: false` does NOT disable this — it only disables a separate curated model list. The two caching systems are independent
- Even with a fresh disk cache, a cold process (new container, restart) has no warm in-memory cache and hits the network

**Suggested fix**

Three approaches, in order of preference:

### A. Config option to disable models.dev network fetch
Add `models_dev.enabled: false` that skips the network stage entirely and only serves from disk cache.

### B. Asynchronous / background refresh
Serve cached data instantly, refresh models.dev in the background. Cache expiry drives refresh, never picker latency.

### C. Shorter connect timeout
Reduce the connect timeout so unreachable hosts fail in <1s instead of 13–15s.

**Workaround (not a fix):**
```bash
echo "127.0.0.1 models.dev" >> /etc/hosts
```
Makes the connection fail instantly (<0.05s). Must be re-applied after every container rebuild.

items.body:
# `delegation.model` is a start-up snapshot: mid-session `hermes config set` silently has no effect

## Summary

`delegation.model` / `delegation.provider` are read **once at process start** into
`cli.CLI_CONFIG` and never re-read. A `hermes config set delegation.model …` issued
during a running session writes `config.yaml` correctly, `hermes config` shows the new
value — but every `delegate_task` child in that session keeps inheriting the **parent's**
model.

There is no warning and no way to tell from inside the session. The only ground truth is
the `Model:` line in the delegation completion banner, which is easy to miss.

This is a cost and correctness problem, not just a papercut: pinning subagents to a
cheap model and unknowingly running them on an expensive one is a silent budget
overrun, and the reverse (expecting a strong model, silently getting a weak one)
degrades output that a human then trusts.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent, git-installed at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`
- macOS 26.5.2
- Provider: AWS Bedrock, models `eu.anthropic.claude-opus-5` / `eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`
- Repo-defined agent personas in `.claude/agents/*.md` (see second issue below)

## Root cause (read out of the source, not inferred)

`tools/delegate_tool.py:2774-2796`:

```python
def _load_config() -> dict:
    """Load delegation config from CLI_CONFIG or persistent config. ..."""
    try:
        from cli import CLI_CONFIG

        cfg = CLI_CONFIG.get("delegation") or {}
        if cfg:
            return cfg          # <-- returns here; config.yaml is never consulted
    except Exception:
        pass
    try:
        from hermes_cli.config import load_config

        full = load_config()
        return full.get("delegation") or {}
    except Exception:
        return {}
```

`cli.py:719`:

```python
CLI_CONFIG = load_cli_config()      # module level -> evaluated once, at import
```

So whenever a `delegation` block exists in the snapshot (it does, by default), the
`load_config()` fallback is unreachable, and `CLI_CONFIG` itself is never refreshed.
The child then falls back to the parent model at `tools/delegate_tool.py:1125`:

```python
effective_model = model or parent_agent.model
```

The docstring of `_load_config()` states the intent — *"so that `delegation.model` /
`delegation.provider` are picked up regardless of the entry point"* — which is exactly
what the early `return cfg` prevents for a mid-session change.

## Reproduction

```bash
# 1. start a session (note the parent model, e.g. Opus)
hermes

# 2. from inside the session (or another shell) change the delegation pin:
hermes config set delegation.model <a-clearly-different-model>
hermes config          # shows the new value -> looks applied

# 3. in the SAME session, dispatch a subagent
#    -> completion banner reports the PARENT model, not the pinned one
```

## Measured behaviour (4 dispatches, same machine, same day)

The distinguishing variable is whether `config.yaml` was written **before or after**
the session process started. `ps -p <pid> -o lstart=` vs. `stat` on `config.yaml`:

| config.yaml written | session start | pin honoured? | child model |
|---|---|---|---|
| mid-session | earlier | **no** | parent's model |
| 12:29 | 12:38:15 | yes | `eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` |
| 13:13:32 | 13:14:04 | yes | `eu.anthropic.claude-opus-5` |
| 14:00:52 | 14:01:35 | yes | `eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` |

Every "yes" row had the write **before** process start; the "no" row had it after.
This is consistent with the snapshot mechanism above and rules out a provider-side or
model-name issue.

Note: an earlier reading of these symptoms concluded "`delegation.model` is ignored
entirely". That is wrong and worth stating explicitly, because it sends people looking
in the wrong place — the value *is* used, it is just captured too early.

## Suggested fixes (in order of preference)

1. **Re-read the persistent config on each `delegate_task` invocation**, or merge
   `load_config()` over the snapshot instead of returning early. Delegation happens
   at most a handful of times per turn — the file read is negligible compared to an
   LLM call.
2. **Make the snapshot semantics visible.** If the effective child model differs from
   `delegation.model` as currently present in `config.yaml`, emit a one-line warning at
   dispatch time (e.g. *"delegation.model in config.yaml is X but this session was
   started with Y; restart to apply"*). This alone would have saved the debugging time.
3. **Have `hermes config set delegation.*` state that a restart is required**, the way
   other snapshot-at-import settings already do (`security.redact_secrets` documents
   this behaviour explicitly in the docs).

## Related, but a separate request: `.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter is not read

Repo-defined agent personas carry an explicit `model:` field, e.g.:

```yaml
---
name: datona-reviewer
tools: Read, Bash
model: arn:aws:bedrock:eu-west-1:…:inference-profile/eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
---
```

A grep over the whole source tree finds **no** reference to `.claude/agents` — the
frontmatter is never consulted, so the model choice a repo has already expressed per
persona has to be re-pinned by hand (and, per the bug above, only before session start).

Honouring `model:` from those files when a delegation is briefed as that persona would
remove the manual pinning step entirely. Filing this as a note rather than a separate
issue since it shares the same underlying surface; happy to split it out if preferred.

## Relation to existing issues

- **#51540** (`delegation.model` ignored for opencode-go provider) — same *symptom*,
  different cause. That report traces it to `_resolve_delegation_credentials()`
  hardcoding `provider = "custom"` when `delegation.base_url` is set, and is
  provider-specific. The mechanism described here is provider-independent (reproduced on
  AWS Bedrock, no `base_url` set) and sits one level earlier, in `_load_config()`. Fixing
  one will not fix the other.
- **#62665** (parent session model contaminated by delegation model after subagent
  failures) — adjacent area (`effective_model` / parent-child model plumbing) but the
  opposite direction of contamination.
- **#72394 / #66536 / #71245** (per-call model override on `delegate_task`) — a per-call
  parameter would sidestep the snapshot entirely and would be a fine alternative fix
  path, but the current documented knob should not silently no-op in the meantime.

## Workaround for other users, until fixed

Set the pin **before** starting the session, and verify it:

```bash
ps -p <session-pid> -o lstart=            # when did the process start?
stat -f "%Sm" ~/.hermes/config.yaml       # when was the pin last written?
# config older than process start  -> pin is in the snapshot, will be honoured
# config newer than process start  -> pin will NOT apply this session
```

And always read the `Model:` line in the delegation completion banner rather than
trusting `hermes config`.

items.title: PYTHONPATH leaks into terminal-tool subprocesses on macOS/Linux, can crash unrelated third-party apps
items.body:
## Summary

`tools/environments/local.py::_ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS` strips `VIRTUAL_ENV` and `CONDA_PREFIX` from every subprocess spawned by the `terminal` tool (the local-backend "managed subprocess environment" path used by `_make_run_env()`, `_sanitize_subprocess_env()`, and `hermes_subprocess_env()`), but **not `PYTHONPATH`**. Hermes' own `PYTHONPATH` (pointing at its bundled venv's `site-packages`) leaks into every command the agent runs via `terminal`, including launches of unrelated third-party applications.

This is not theoretical — it crash-looped a real macOS app (ComfyUI Desktop) in production use, twice in the same user session, and the agent's own attempted "fix" (clearing `PYTHONPATH` via `launchctl` system-wide) made things worse before the actual cause was found.

## Reproduction (macOS, current `main`)

```
$ hermes -z "Run this exact terminal command and show me the raw output: echo \"PYTHONPATH='\$PYTHONPATH'\""
Raw output:
PYTHONPATH='/Users/…/.hermes/hermes-agent:/Users/…/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages'
```

Any subprocess launched through the `terminal` tool inherits this. In the field incident, the agent ran `open -a "Comfy Desktop"` to (re)start ComfyUI Desktop. ComfyUI Desktop runs its own bundled Python 3.13 venv, but inherited Hermes' `PYTHONPATH` and tried to import PIL's compiled C-extension from Hermes' Python 3.11 venv instead of its own:

```
File ".../ComfyUI/comfy_execution/progress.py", line 3, in <module>
    from PIL import Image
File ".../hermes-agent/venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/PIL/Image.py", line 95, in <module>
    from . import _imaging as core
ImportError: cannot import name '_imaging' from 'PIL' (.../hermes-agent/venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/PIL/__init__.py)
```

ComfyUI Desktop crash-looped every time it was (re)launched from a Hermes-spawned subprocess, for the duration of the session.

## Why existing fixes didn't catch this

- PR #45501 ("fix: cron model.default fallback + VIRTUAL_ENV leak into subprocesses") added `VIRTUAL_ENV`, `VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT`, `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT`, `POETRY_ACTIVE`, `PIPENV_ACTIVE`, `CONDA_PREFIX`, `CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV` to `_HERMES_PROVIDER_ENV_BLOCKLIST` — a **different list**, used for provider-credential stripping, not the active-venv-marker stripping that `_make_run_env()` / `_sanitize_subprocess_env()` / `hermes_subprocess_env()` actually apply via `_ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS`.
- #58382 independently found `CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV` missing from the *correct* list (`_ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS`) via source review, confirming it's still just `(VIRTUAL_ENV, CONDA_PREFIX)` on current `main`. `PYTHONPATH` has the same gap and is arguably higher-impact, since every Python interpreter (not just venv-aware tools like `uv`/`poetry`) unconditionally consults it — it doesn't need a venv-aware tool in the child process to bite.
- #65909 and #57467 report the same underlying symptom (`PYTHONPATH` leaking into child processes) but are filed as Windows-specific, pointing at `_ensure_windows_gateway_venv_imports` in the gateway. This report confirms the leak also reproduces on **macOS**, through the separate `tools/environments/local.py` terminal-tool spawn path — so there appear to be at least two independent leak sources (Windows gateway venv-import shimming, and the cross-platform local-terminal env copy) that both need the fix, not one.

## Fix

Add `PYTHONPATH` to `_ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS` in `tools/environments/local.py` (and, per #58382, `CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV` while touching this):

```diff
- _ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS = ("VIRTUAL_ENV", "CONDA_PREFIX")
+ _ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS = ("VIRTUAL_ENV", "CONDA_PREFIX", "PYTHONPATH")
```

Verified locally: after this change, `echo "PYTHONPATH='$PYTHONPATH'"` run via the `terminal` tool returns an empty value, and the Hermes venv itself stays reachable (its `bin/` is first on `PATH`), consistent with the existing rationale already documented above `_ACTIVE_VENV_MARKER_VARS` for why stripping these markers is safe.

## Suggested severity

P1/P2 — this doesn't just misconfigure an inherited package manager (the `VIRTUAL_ENV`/`CONDA_PREFIX` cases); it can directly crash arbitrary third-party GUI applications that a user asks the agent to launch or interact with, with no indication to the model that its own environment is the cause (the resulting traceback points entirely at the target app, not at Hermes).

labels.name: comp/cli

items.body:
## Expected behavior

`pyproject.toml` declares three `[project.scripts]` entries:

```
hermes = "hermes_cli.main:main"
hermes-agent = "run_agent:main"
hermes-acp = "acp_adapter.entry:main"
```

The ACP docs (`website/docs/user-guide/features/acp.md`) list `hermes acp`, `hermes-acp`, and `python -m acp_adapter` as equally supported ways to launch ACP mode, with no caveat that `hermes-acp` requires extra setup.

## Actual behavior

`scripts/install.sh`'s `setup_path()` only ever generates a `hermes` launcher in the command-link directory (`~/.local/bin` on macOS/Linux non-root, `/usr/local/bin` for root/FHS). `hermes-agent` and `hermes-acp` are built correctly into `venv/bin/` by the editable install but are never linked into the user's PATH, so external tools that expect `hermes-acp` as a standalone command can't find it even after a fully successful install.

Neither `hermes update` nor `hermes doctor` fill this gap — `hermes update` re-installs the venv (regenerating `venv/bin/hermes-acp`) but never touches the command-link directory, and the `.exe` shim quarantine logic in `hermes_cli/main.py` (`_hermes_exe_shims`) is Windows-only and returns `[]` on POSIX.

## Reproduction

Confirmed on a completely clean `git clone` + fresh venv (not just the reporter's existing install):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent.git
cd hermes-agent
uv venv venv
uv pip install -e . --python venv/bin/python
ls venv/bin/hermes*
# → hermes, hermes-acp, hermes-agent all present
```

Then extracting and running `setup_path()` from `scripts/install.sh` against that fresh venv with a fresh command-link directory produces only:

```
$COMMAND_LINK_DIR/hermes
```

`hermes-acp` and `hermes-agent` are absent. This confirms the gap is a property of `setup_path()` itself, not environment-specific drift.

## Evidence

- `pyproject.toml:308-311` — three declared console scripts
- `scripts/install.sh:1657-1678` — single hard-coded `cat > "$command_link_dir/hermes"`, no equivalent for the other two
- `git log --all -S "hermes-acp" -- scripts/install.sh` — zero matches; this isn't a regression, the string has never appeared in that file's history
- `website/docs/user-guide/features/acp.md:42-62` — docs present `hermes-acp` as first-tier supported with no setup caveat

Current evidence is most consistent with an installer omission, but I can't establish intent from source alone — flagging as observed behavior only, no proposed fix attached.

items.title: [Bug]: Update didn't finish
[Bug]: macOS in-app update permanently broken by a stale leftover ~/.hermes/hermes-setup — resolveUpdaterBinary() has no version gate and nothing refreshes the binary

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
### Bug Description

On macOS, a **leftover `~/.hermes/hermes-setup` binary from an old install permanently breaks the in-app Update button**, and no amount of `hermes update` can repair it.

`resolveUpdaterBinary()` gates purely on file existence, with no version or staleness check:

```js
// apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2604
function resolveUpdaterBinary() {
  const name = IS_WINDOWS ? 'hermes-setup.exe' : 'hermes-setup'
  const candidate = path.join(HERMES_HOME, name)

  return fileExists(candidate) ? candidate : null
}
```

So any macOS install that ever acquired a `hermes-setup` binary is routed into the Windows-style quit→hand-off→rebuild dance instead of the native `applyUpdatesPosixInApp` path — using a binary that may be months old. Mine is from **2026-06-08**, predating the `HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID` contract added in `8c76fe19f` to fix #74761.

Net effect: **the fix for #74761 cannot reach existing installs.** `hermes update` refreshes the Python side, which now honors the hand-off — but nothing in the repo ever refreshes the prebuilt `hermes-setup` binary that is supposed to *send* it. Users on the newest `main` still see the #74761 symptom, so it reads as "the fix didn't work".

Each failed attempt also writes a full pre-update state snapshot first — I accumulated 3 × 378.6 MB = **1.1 GB** of `state.db.pre-update-emergency-*.bak` purely from retries.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a macOS install that owns a `~/.hermes/hermes-setup` predating `8c76fe19f` (e.g. a June-era install)
2. Run `hermes update` to any current `main` — the Python side now honors the hand-off
3. Click Update in the desktop app
4. "UPDATE DIDN'T FINISH — Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again."
5. Click **Retry update**. Identical failure, every time, indefinitely

### Expected Behavior

Either the stale `hermes-setup` is refreshed / version-gated and ignored, or the desktop falls through to the native macOS `applyUpdatesPosixInApp` path. The updater should not treat its own orchestrating parent as a rival update, and a binary that cannot honor the current hand-off contract should not be selected to drive the update.

### Actual Behavior

The updater deadlocks against itself and the error is misleading — no Hermes window or Electron process was running in any of my attempts.

```
12:43:18.205070Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib: Hermes installer starting mode=Update force_setup=false
12:43:19.245319Z  INFO bootstrap.log: ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 17907, started 1s ago).
12:43:19.263542Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib::update: update stage stage=update state=Failed duration_ms=Some(533) error=Some("Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again.")
12:43:20.471550Z  INFO bootstrap.log: ✗ Another Hermes update is already running (PID 17907, started 2s ago).
12:43:20.489484Z  INFO hermes_bootstrap_lib::update: update stage stage=update state=Failed duration_ms=Some(152) error=Some("Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again.")
```

PID 17907 *is* the process reporting the conflict. Reproduced with updater PIDs 3868, 3961, 5048 and 17907 across ~8.5 hours — deterministic, and Retry can never win.

### Affected Component

Setup / Installation, Other (Desktop app / bootstrap-installer)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Not uploaded — `hermes debug share` pushes config and logs to a public paste service,
which I'd rather not do for this install. Everything relevant is quoted inline:
environment fields below, bootstrap-installer.log excerpts above, and the
verification commands under Root Cause Analysis. Happy to add the links on request.
```

### Operating System

macOS 27.0 (build 26A5388g), Apple Silicon (arm64)

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.19.0 (2026.7.20) · upstream b4f8c491 — install method: git (`~/.hermes/hermes-agent`)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell
# The shipped binary has no knowledge of the hand-off contract:
$ ls -la ~/.hermes/hermes-setup
-rwxr-xr-x  1 user  staff  11324400 Jun  8 21:49 /Users/user/.hermes/hermes-setup

$ strings ~/.hermes/hermes-setup | grep -i HANDOFF
$ echo $?
1

# ...while the checkout it drives does:
$ grep -n HANDOFF_PID_ENV hermes_cli/update_lock.py
64:HANDOFF_PID_ENV = "HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID"

$ grep -n HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID apps/bootstrap-installer/src-tauri/src/update.rs
919:        "HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID".to_string(),
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

1. Old `hermes-setup` (PID *N*) claims the marker with **its own** pid — `UpdateMarkerGuard::acquire()`, `apps/bootstrap-installer/src-tauri/src/update.rs:201-210`
2. It spawns `hermes update --yes --gateway --force` — `update.rs:354-369`
3. Being pre-`8c76fe19f`, it never exports `HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID` (`update_child_env`, `update.rs:919`)
4. The child's `UpdateLock.acquire()` (`hermes_cli/main.py:8998`) reads the marker, sees pid *N* alive at age 0s, finds no hand-off env var → treats its own parent as a rival → `sys.exit(2)` (`UPDATE_EXIT_CONCURRENT`)
5. Rust maps exit 2 → `"Hermes is still running. Close all Hermes windows and try the update again."` — `update.rs:423-425`

`--force` does not help: the lock gate runs before `_cmd_update_impl`, so that flag does not cover it.

The delivery gap: nothing on macOS ever rewrites the binary. `scripts/install.sh` does not place it, and only the Windows path self-copies `hermes-setup.exe` into `HERMES_HOME` (`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2598`).

### Proposed Fix (optional)

1. **Version-gate `resolveUpdaterBinary()`** instead of testing existence — stamp the binary with its build commit (`scripts/install.ps1:1515` notes it already bakes one) and ignore or refresh a binary older than the hand-off contract. Narrowest fix.
2. **Refresh `hermes-setup` during `hermes update`**, or at minimum warn when the on-disk binary is older than the checkout it is expected to drive.
3. **Make the Python side not depend on a binary it cannot update** — when `HERMES_UPDATE_HANDOFF_PID` is absent, fall back to detecting an orchestrating `hermes-setup` *ancestor*. Still pid-matched against the live marker owner, so it grants nothing the env var doesn't. I'm running this locally as a bridge and it resolves the deadlock with the old binary in place.

**Workarounds** for anyone hitting this now — run the update in a terminal, where no parent holds the marker:

```bash
hermes update
```

Or restore the intended macOS path so `resolveUpdaterBinary()` returns `null`:

```bash
mv ~/.hermes/hermes-setup ~/.hermes/hermes-setup.stale.bak
```

Related: #74761 (the marker self-refusal this fixed — closed), #74531 (same user-facing symptom, still open).

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: fix(openviking): missing cooldown on unreachable health state causes spawn loop (DataDirectoryLocked every 2-5 min)

labels.name: area/memory
labels.description: Memory subsystem: store, providers, sync, background reviews

items.body:
## Bug Description

The OpenViking memory plugin auto-start mechanism enters a spawn loop when the health check returns `"unreachable"` (timeout/connection error) while the server is actually running. A new `openviking-server` process is spawned every ~5 minutes, each hitting `DataDirectoryLocked` and exiting immediately.

## Root Cause (revised)

~~Was: missing cooldown on `"unreachable"` branch in `_ensure_client_locked()`~~

**Actual**: The `_failed_refresh` cooldown (30s, L2439) IS already applied to both `"responded"` and `"unreachable"` branches. The cooldown works but is insufficient — after 30s it expires and the cycle repeats.

The real root cause is in `_start_local_openviking_server()`: it **blindly spawns a new process without checking whether the server is already running**. Two call sites trigger this:

| Call site | When | 
|---|---|
| `initialize()` L2339 | Gateway startup |
| `_ensure_client_locked()` L2447 | Every health check cycle |

Both paths converge at `_start_local_openviking_server()` → `subprocess.Popen()` with no pre-flight check.

### Why health check returns "unreachable" despite server running

`_classify_runtime_openviking_health()` uses `_VikingClient.health()` with a default httpx timeout. The server IS running (`curl /health` returns 200), but the client-side health check sometimes times out → returns `"unreachable"` → triggers spawn.

## Reproduction

1. Run `openviking-server` on `127.0.0.1:1933`
2. Configure Hermes with `memory.provider: openviking`
3. Observe OV logs: `DataDirectoryLocked` every ~5 minutes despite server running

## Proposed Fix

In `_start_local_openviking_server()`, check whether the server is already listening on the target `host:port` **before** spawning:

```python
def _start_local_openviking_server(endpoint: str) -> tuple[bool, str]:
+   # Check if server is already running before spawning
+   try:
+       host, port = _local_openviking_bind(endpoint)
+   except ValueError as e:
+       return False, f"Could not parse local OpenViking URL: {e}"
+   try:
+       _sock = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=2.0)
+       _sock.close()
+       return True, f"OpenViking server is already running on {host}:{port}."
+   except OSError:
+       pass  # not reachable — proceed with spawn
+
    server_cmd = shutil.which("openviking-server")
    ...
```

This covers ALL call paths because both `initialize()` and `_ensure_client_locked()` go through this function.

### Why this approach

- **Minimal**: 10 lines, no new dependencies
- **Complete**: covers both call sites (unlike a cooldown-only fix)
- **Fast**: 2s timeout socket check vs 15s health check waiter
- **Defense-in-depth**: complements the existing 30s cooldown

## Verified

Locally patched and tested on `b4f8c491d`:
- **Before**: ~18 DataDirectoryLocked/day, spawn every ~5 min
- **After**: 0 spawns in 21+ minutes of observation

## Environment

- Commit: `b4f8c491d`
- Config: `memory.provider: openviking`, endpoint `http://127.0.0.1:1933/mcp`
- OpenViking: 0.4.11

items.title: feat: Route explicit wake-word commands to existing Desktop sessions

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Problem or Use Case

Hermes Desktop can currently:

- route a detected wake phrase to a profile and optionally start a fresh session (`wake.detected`, #70509), and
- send typed Quick Entry text to a selected existing session (#72315).

It cannot explicitly select an existing Desktop conversation from the first wake-triggered spoken turn. A request such as:

> “Hey Hermes — send to the resume session: review the experience section.”

is submitted to whichever fresh/current session the global `wake_word.start_new_session` setting selected. Users with several concurrent Desktop conversations therefore have no safe hands-free way to address one by title.

Routing to the wrong conversation is materially worse than declining to route: it can alter unrelated work, leak context across tasks, or resume a session owned by another profile. Related work such as #17193 and #65448/#64436 is broader cross-surface session management/injection; #57106 also shows why title-based `/resume` should not be the dispatch mechanism.

## Proposed Solution

Add a narrowly scoped **Desktop-only** explicit routing step for the first transcript started by `wake.detected`:

1. Preserve the existing wake phrase → profile routing behavior.
2. Mark the resulting one-shot main-composer voice start as wake-triggered.
3. Parse only explicit commands, initially along the lines of:
   - `send to <session title> session: <prompt>`
   - `continue in <session title> session: <prompt>`
4. Resolve candidates from non-archived sessions in the active profile using a deterministic ladder:
   - exact normalized title;
   - unique normalized title prefix;
   - otherwise reject as missing or ambiguous.
5. Resume/foreground the resolved stored session through the existing Desktop session lifecycle, then submit through the ordinary composer path so streaming state and spoken replies remain bound to the destination session.
6. If the destination is missing, ambiguous, stale, or fails to resume, do **not** silently fall back to another session. Surface a recoverable notification and continue listening.
7. If the first transcript is not an explicit routing command, preserve current behavior byte-for-byte.

No LLM or unconstrained fuzzy matching is needed for v1. Users can already rename a session to a short voice-friendly title, so a separate alias persistence/settings system can be a follow-up if real usage proves it necessary.

### Scope and invariants

- Desktop renderer only; no new gateway RPC or model tool.
- First wake-triggered transcript only. Manual Voice Mode and tile composers are unchanged.
- Candidate lookup is scoped to the active profile; no cross-profile fallback.
- Canonical stored/runtime session identities are translated at the existing resume boundary; do not dispatch via `/resume <title>`.
- Explicit user routing may foreground the destination, but background events without explicit routing must never steal focus.
- Existing `wake_word.start_new_session` behavior remains the fallback for ordinary wake utterances.

### Test plan

- parser preserves the original prompt text;
- exact title match;
- Unicode/case/whitespace normalization;
- unique prefix match;
- duplicate exact titles are ambiguous;
- multiple prefix matches are ambiguous;
- missing and archived targets are rejected;
- sessions from another profile are excluded;
- a non-routing utterance passes through unchanged;
- only the first wake-triggered transcript is eligible;
- manual Voice Mode is unchanged;
- resume/submit failure cannot fall back to the old/current session;
- rejected routing returns the voice loop to listening instead of leaving it waiting for an assistant reply that will never arrive.

## Alternatives Considered

### Reuse Quick Entry's background session delegate directly

Quick Entry provides the correct stored → runtime identity translation, but a background send alone is not sufficient for a live voice turn: the voice loop would keep observing the old main session and wait indefinitely for a reply there. Foregrounding through the normal resume path keeps transcript streaming and TTS attached to the actual destination.

### Route through `/resume <title>`

Rejected because matching and identity behavior are not strict enough for a safety-sensitive send, and #57106 reports orphan/fork behavior around resume-by-name. Resolve a stored session deterministically and use existing canonical session APIs instead.

### LLM intent classification / fuzzy title guessing

Rejected for v1. It adds latency and can silently choose the wrong conversation. Exact and unique-prefix matching are observable and testable.

### Add persistent aliases immediately

Useful later, but it expands settings, persistence, profile-scoping, and migration surface before the routing lifecycle is proven. Renamed session titles provide a zero-infrastructure first version.

## Related work

- #70509 — wake phrase profile routing
- #72315 — Quick Entry targeting existing sessions
- #17193 — cross-session management across surfaces
- #57106 — resume-by-name identity problem
- #65448 / #64436 — gateway/plugin injection into an existing session
- #66091 — configured handoff destinations (platform/channel routing, not Desktop conversation routing)

## Feature Type

Other — Hermes Desktop voice/session UX

## Scope

Medium (a small pure resolver plus focused Desktop wiring and tests)

## Contribution

I’d like to implement this and submit a PR.

items.body:
### Bug Description

**Describe the bug**
When Hermes Gateway runs with the Weixin (WeChat) platform via iLink (ilinkai.weixin.qq.com), there are intermittent windows lasting hours where outbound messages are silently dropped by iLink. Gateway logs show "Sending response" / "Sending image" successfully with no errors, but the user never receives them. The only recovery is the user sending a new message.
**Environment**
- Hermes version: 0.19.0
- Platform: Weixin (WeChat) via iLink (ilinkai.weixin.qq.com)
- Container: Docker 65b4b4753e5e (s6 supervisor)
- Model: sensenova-6.7-flash-lite
- Gateway command: `gateway run --replace`

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run Gateway with Weixin/iLink connected
2. Gateway processes a user request (e.g., image generation) and completes
3. Gateway logs "Sending response (N chars)" and "Sending image: file://..." successfully
4. User waits — **message never arrives**
5. User re-sends a message — Gateway processes it and user finally gets a reply
6. Gap between last successful Gateway log and next received message: **2+ hours** in observed case

### Expected Behavior

Messages should reach the user reliably. If the WebSocket degrades or iLink silently drops messages, Gateway should detect this, log an error, and attempt to reconnect or at least warn.

### Actual Behavior

Gateway considers delivery successful, logs "Sending response/image", but iLink silently consumes the messages without delivering to WeChat. No error in `gateway.log` or `errors.log`. Gateway only recovers when a new inbound user message arrives.

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
**Timeline (CST) — 2026-07-30**
Time	Event
16:13:21	User sends message
16:16:59	Gateway logs "Sending response (396 chars)" + "Sending image" — appears successful
16:17 → 18:23	**2h06m — user receives nothing, Gateway idle, no errors**
18:23:24	User sends "没有反应？"
18:23:42	Gateway responds — user finally receives it
**Key logs:**

16:16:59,495 [Weixin] Sending response (396 chars) to o9cq80_...
16:16:59,958 [Weixin] Sending image: file:///opt/data/cache/images/studio_singer_16_9_v3.png (alt=)
< 2+ hours of silence >
18:23:42,223 [Weixin] Sending response (59 chars)
18:23:42,536 [Weixin] Sending image: file:///opt/data/cache/images/studio_singer_16_9_v3.png

**Diagnosis**
This is **not** a Docker/s6 issue (no SIGTERM, Gateway alive throughout). The drop happens on the **Gateway → iLink WebSocket → WeChat** path. Likely: iLink WebSocket silently times out during idle without notifying Gateway, so Gateway has no signal the connection is dead.
**Suggested fix**
```

### Bug Description

The desktop client intermittently fails to connect to its own backend with
`Could not connect to Hermes gateway` / `Hermes couldn't start`, and then enters a
**repair loop**: the renderer detects a transient WebSocket failure, asks the
bootstrap to "repair", and the bootstrap force-reinstalls + restarts the backend —
which stalls again, repeating forever.

Manually starting `hermes serve` *outside* the desktop and then opening the desktop
is stable. This shows the problem is **not** corrupted config, but the desktop's
aggressive backend lifecycle management reacting to a transient backend stall.

### Steps to Reproduce

**Basic:**
1. On a clean/installed Windows instance, launch the desktop (`Hermes.exe`).
2. Let the desktop **spawn its own backend** (do not pre-start `hermes serve`).
3. Wait for the backend to run for a while (or drive heavier load), until one
   `event loop stalled` occurs.
4. Observe in `errors.log`: `event loop stalled … (GIL pressure suspected)` →
   `ws ready frame send failed`; and in `desktop.log`:
   `[bootstrap] repair requested by renderer; forcing reinstall`. The desktop shows
   `Could not connect to Hermes gateway` and/or loops reconnecting.

**More reliable (avoid waiting for a random stall):**
1. Pre-start a persistent backend: `hermes serve` (default port `127.0.0.1:9119`).
2. Open the desktop; confirm it connects.
3. Induce GIL pressure on the backend (e.g. churn/unload several MCP servers, or
   sustained heavy concurrent sessions). The WS ready-frame failure + repair loop
   reproduces consistently.

**Environment notes**
- Windows 11, hermes-agent `0.19.0`, Electron desktop.
- Logs: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\logs\errors.log` and `desktop.log`.
- Backend default port `9119` (`--port 0` = random; the desktop probes `9119`).

### Expected Behavior

Observed failure chain (in time order), from the local logs:

1. `hermes serve` (and the gateway child it re-execs) periodically logs
   `event loop stalled … (GIL pressure suspected)` — up to **14223.7s (≈3.9h)**,
   with many 10–360s stalls.
2. While the loop is stalled, the TUI WebSocket write is slow
   (`ws write slow (loop stalled >10.0s)`), then
   **`ws send failed` → `ws ready frame send failed`** (renderer peer `127.0.0.1:<port>`).
3. The desktop renderer treats the ready-frame failure as a dead backend and
   requests repair:
   `[bootstrap] repair requested by renderer; forcing reinstall …`
4. The bootstrap **tears down the still-alive backend and re-runs the installer**
   (`bypassing the usable active runtime to re-run the installer`), spawning a fresh
   backend that stalls again → another repair → **infinite loop**.

Core contradiction: a *transient* GIL stall is treated as a *fatal* backend fault,
triggering a destructive reinstall instead of waiting/retrying the existing backend.

Note: `hermes serve` re-execs a real gateway child process (observed: parent is the
venv python, the child lands on the uv-managed `cpython-3.11`). The child's runtime
stability drives stall frequency — worth investigating its Windows GIL pressure at
startup (heavy synchronous work: heavy imports, web-UI build, or MCP discovery
blocking the event loop).


### Actual Behavior

Keep one stable backend alive **before** the desktop opens, so the desktop attaches
to the existing backend instead of spawning + repairing its own:

- Pre-start `hermes serve` (default `127.0.0.1:9119`), then open the desktop; **or**
- A launcher that kills stale Hermes processes →
  `venv\Scripts\python.exe -m hermes_cli.main serve` → launches `Hermes.exe`;
- Place that "backend-only" launcher in the Windows Startup folder
  (`%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup`) so a backend is always
  resident on login.

> This only *masks* the loop/error spam; the underlying transient stall remains. A

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)
